Redraw the network as four nodes and solve; the symmetry collapses it to **10 Ω**.
**Step 1 — name the nodes.** Besides A and B, call the left-hand junction **Q** and the
top-right junction **R** ✓
**Step 2 — list the branches.** Tracing the figure, each branch is built from 10 Ω
resistors:
A-R: **10 Ω** (the middle vertical)
A-Q: **10 Ω** (the middle horizontal)
Q-R: **20 Ω** (left 10 Ω then top 10 Ω in series)
Q-B: **10 Ω** (down the left side, along the bottom 10 Ω)
R-B: **10 Ω** (the right-hand resistor) ✓
**Step 3 — solve by node potentials.** Put V_B = 0 and inject current at A, with
V_A = V, V_Q = q, V_R = r.
at Q: (V − q)/10 + (r − q)/20 − q/10 = 0, giving **2V + r = 5q** ✓
at R: (V − r)/10 + (q − r)/20 − r/10 = 0, giving **2V + q = 5r** ✓
**Step 4 — exploit the symmetry.** Subtracting the two equations:
r − q = 5q − 5r, so **r = q** ✓ - the bridge is **balanced**, and no current flows in
the 20 Ω between them.
**Step 5 — finish.** With r = q, the first equation gives
2V + q = 5q, so **q = V/2** ✓
current from A: (V − q)/10 + (V − r)/10 = 2(V/2)/10 = **V/10**
**R_AB = V/(V/10) = 10 Ω** ✓
**The shortcut once balance is seen.** With no current in the Q-R branch, it can be
**deleted** ✓ What remains is
A-R-B: 10 + 10 = **20 Ω**
A-Q-B: 10 + 10 = **20 Ω**
two 20 Ω paths in **parallel**: 20/2 = **10 Ω** ✓ the answer in one line.
**Why the bridge balances.** The two paths from A to B are **identical** - 10 Ω then
10 Ω each ✓ so Q and R sit at the same potential and the connecting branch is idle.
Spotting such symmetry is the single most useful skill in network problems.
**Why a balanced branch may be removed or short-circuited.** Either operation changes
nothing, since it carries no current and has no voltage across it ✓ Both routes give
the same answer, which is a useful check.
**A sanity bound.** The answer must lie **below** the 20 Ω of a single path and
**above** the resistance of the whole network short-circuited ✓ 10 Ω sits sensibly
between.
∴ 10 Ω.

To make a voltmeter, add a **large resistance in series**.
**Step 1 — write the condition.** At full-scale deflection the whole 20 V must drive
the full-scale current through the galvanometer and the added resistance together:
V = I_g(G + R) ✓
**Step 2 — rearrange.**
R = V/I_g − G ✓
**Step 3 — substitute.**
R = 20/(5 x 10⁻³) − 50
= 4000 − 50
= **3950 Ω**, in **series** ✓
**Why series and not parallel.** A voltmeter must draw as **little** current as
possible ✓ A large series resistance raises the instrument's total resistance to
4000 Ω, so it disturbs the circuit it measures very little. A **parallel** resistor
would do the opposite - that is how an **ammeter** is made.
**Why subtracting G matters.** It changes 4000 to **3950** ✓ under 1·3%, but both
values appear among the options, so the question is testing exactly that step.
**The finished instrument's resistance.** **4000 Ω** for a 20 V range ✓
**Its sensitivity.**
4000/20 = **200 Ω per volt** ✓ the standard way of rating an analogue voltmeter - the
higher the figure, the less the instrument loads the circuit.
**How to make other ranges.** For 0-100 V:
R = 100/0·005 − 50 = **19950 Ω** ✓ A multi-range voltmeter simply switches between such
resistors.
**The ammeter conversion, for contrast.** To read 0-1 A one would add a **shunt** in
parallel:
S = I_gG/(I − I_g) = (0·005)(50)/0·995 = **0·251 Ω** ✓ a tiny resistance, keeping the
ammeter's total resistance low.
**Why the galvanometer alone is useless as a voltmeter.** Across 20 V it would pass
20/50 = **0·4 A** ✓ eighty times its full-scale current - and would burn out instantly.
**The loading error.** Connected across a 10 kΩ resistor, this voltmeter would draw
enough current to disturb the reading by about 70% ✓ which is why modern digital
voltmeters have input resistances of 10 MΩ or more.
**Reading the distractors.** **4050 Ω** ✗ **adds** G instead of subtracting it. The two
**parallel** options ✗ would make an ammeter, and would short-circuit the measurement ✓
∴ 3950 Ω in series with galvanometer.

**Curie's law** makes the susceptibility inversely proportional to the absolute
temperature.
**Step 1 — state the law.**
χ = **C/T** ✓
for a paramagnetic material, with C the Curie constant.
**Step 2 — write it for each temperature.**
χ₁ = C/T₁ and χ₂ = C/T₂ ✓
**Step 3 — eliminate C.**
χ₁T₁ = C and χ₂T₂ = C, so
**χ₁T₁ = χ₂T₂** ✓
**Why cooling raises the susceptibility.** Paramagnetism is a contest between the
aligning influence of the applied field and the **randomising** effect of thermal
motion ✓ Cooling weakens the randomisation, so a given field aligns a larger fraction
of the atomic moments.
**The physical origin.** Each atom carries a permanent magnetic moment, normally
pointing at random ✓ The field produces only a slight net alignment - the energy µB is
tiny compared with kT at ordinary temperatures, which is why χ is of order 10⁻⁵.
**A worked instance.** χ = 0·0075 at 200 K:
at 100 K: χ = 0·0075 x 200/100 = **0·015** ✓ doubled by halving the temperature.
**Why T must be in kelvin.** The law is χ ∝ 1/T on the **absolute** scale ✓ Using
celsius would give nonsense - a negative susceptibility below 0 °C.
**What happens as T → 0.** χ grows without limit ✓ In practice the law fails at very
low temperatures, where the moments begin to interact and the material may order
magnetically; χ then saturates, since the magnetisation cannot exceed full alignment.
**The ferromagnetic version.** Above the Curie point,
χ = **C/(T − T_C)** ✓ the Curie-Weiss law - the same 1/T character, shifted by the
ordering temperature. Below T_C the material is ferromagnetic and no simple law
applies.
**The contrast with diamagnetism.** Diamagnetic susceptibility is **independent** of
temperature ✓ because it arises from induced currents in the electron orbits, not from
the alignment of permanent moments.
**How the law was found.** Pierre Curie, 1895, from measurements on oxygen and other
paramagnetic gases ✓ It was one of the first quantitative laws of magnetism, and
Langevin explained it statistically ten years later.
**Reading the distractors.** **χ₁ = χ₂** ✗ ignores the temperature dependence.
**χ₁T₂ = χ₂T₁** ✗ makes χ **proportional** to T, the reverse. **χ₁√T₁ = χ₂√T₂** ✗
invents a square root ✓
∴ χ₁T₁ = χ₂T₂.

The horizontal component is **B cos δ**, so the total field is **B_H/cos δ**.
**Step 1 — state the relation.**
B_H = B cos δ ✓
with δ the angle of **dip**, measured from the horizontal.
**Step 2 — rearrange.**
B = B_H/cos δ ✓
**Step 3 — substitute.**
B = 3·0/cos 30°
= 3·0/0·866 ✓
**Step 4 — evaluate.**
= **3·46 ≈ 3·5 G** ✓
**Why the total field exceeds the horizontal component.** The Earth's field dips
**below** the horizontal, so part of it is vertical ✓ The horizontal part is only a
projection, and the whole is always the larger.
**The vertical component.**
B_V = B sin δ = 3·46 x 0·5 = **1·73 G** ✓
and a check: √(3·0² + 1·73²) = √(9 + 3) = **3·46 G** ✓ consistent.
**The three elements of terrestrial magnetism.**
**declination**: the angle between geographic and magnetic north ✓
**dip (inclination)**: the angle of the field below the horizontal ✓
**horizontal intensity** B_H ✓
Together they specify the field completely at any point.
**How dip varies with latitude.**
magnetic **equator**: δ = **0°**, the field is horizontal ✓
magnetic **poles**: δ = **90°**, the field is vertical and B_H = 0 ✓
mid-latitudes: intermediate - δ = 30° places this location fairly near the equator.
**Why a compass fails near the poles.** B_H → 0, so there is no horizontal field to
align the needle ✓ Navigation there must use gyroscopes or satellites.
**The dip circle.** A compass needle free to rotate in a **vertical** plane ✓ aligned
with the magnetic meridian it reads the dip directly - the standard instrument for
measuring δ.
**A sense of scale.** The Earth's total field is about **0·25 to 0·65 G**, that is
**25 to 65 µT** ✓ The 3 G quoted here is some five times larger than anywhere on
Earth; the question's numbers are chosen for the arithmetic.
**The unit.** 1 gauss = **10⁻⁴ tesla** ✓ the CGS unit, still common in geomagnetism.
**Reading the distractors.** **6·0 G** ✗ is B_H/sin δ, using the wrong function - the
commonest error. **5·1 G** ✗ and **4·5 G** ✗ correspond to dips of 54° and 48° ✓
∴ 3.5 G.

Superimposing a message on a carrier is **modulation**.
**Step 1 — define it.** **Modulation** is the process of varying some property of a
high-frequency **carrier** wave in accordance with a low-frequency **message**
signal ✓
**Step 2 — name the three kinds.**
**amplitude modulation (AM)**: the carrier's **amplitude** follows the message ✓
**frequency modulation (FM)**: its **frequency** does ✓
**phase modulation (PM)**: its **phase** does ✓
**Why modulation is necessary at all.** Three reasons ✓
**antenna size**: an efficient antenna must be about λ/4 long. A 1 kHz audio signal has
λ = 300 km, needing a 75 km antenna - absurd. At 1 MHz, λ = 300 m and the antenna is
75 m, which is practical ✓
**power**: radiated power goes as 1/λ², so low frequencies radiate feebly ✓
**sharing the spectrum**: without modulation every station would occupy the same audio
band and interfere hopelessly ✓
**What AM produces.** A carrier plus **two sidebands** at ν_c ± ν_m ✓ occupying a
bandwidth of twice the highest modulating frequency - which is why medium-wave stations
are spaced 9 or 10 kHz apart.
**Why FM sounds better.** Noise mostly affects **amplitude**, which an FM receiver
ignores ✓ FM broadcasting also uses a much wider bandwidth - 200 kHz against AM's 10 -
allowing full audio fidelity and stereo.
**The reverse process.** **Demodulation** or detection, performed at the receiver ✓ For
AM a simple diode and capacitor suffice, which is why crystal sets need no power supply.
**What the other options mean.**
**amplification** ✗ increases a signal's strength without changing its form ✓
**demodulation** ✗ is the reverse of modulation, recovering the message ✓
**transmission** ✗ is the radiation and propagation of the modulated wave - a later
stage altogether ✓
**The modulation index.** µ = A_m/A_c ✓ For AM it must not exceed 1, or the envelope is
distorted and the message cannot be recovered cleanly - **over-modulation**.
∴ Modulation.

Find the field inside the solenoid, then the energy density **B²/(2µ₀)**.
**Step 1 — convert the turn density.**
40 turns per cm = **4000 turns per metre** ✓
**Step 2 — find the field.**
B = µ₀nI
= (4π x 10⁻⁷)(4000)(1)
= **1·6π x 10⁻³ T** ✓
**Step 3 — apply the energy-density formula.**
u = B²/(2µ₀) ✓
= (1·6π x 10⁻³)²/(2 x 4π x 10⁻⁷) ✓
**Step 4 — evaluate.**
numerator: 2·56π² x 10⁻⁶
denominator: 8π x 10⁻⁷
u = (2·56π²/8π) x 10
= (0·32π) x 10
= **3·2π J m⁻³** ✓
**Step 5 — as a number.** 3·2π = **10·05 J m⁻³** ✓
**A neater route.** Substituting B = µ₀nI into u = B²/2µ₀:
u = **µ₀n²I²/2** ✓
= (4π x 10⁻⁷)(4000)²(1)/2
= (4π x 10⁻⁷)(1·6 x 10⁷)/2
= 6·4π/2
= **3·2π** ✓ the same, with fewer powers of ten to mishandle.
**Why the energy density is uniform inside.** The field of a long solenoid is uniform ✓
so every cubic metre of the interior stores the same energy - which is what makes the
density a useful quantity here.
**The total energy.** Multiply by the volume ✓
For a solenoid 1 m long and 2 cm across: V = 3·14 x 10⁻⁴ m³, so
U = 10·05 x 3·14 x 10⁻⁴ = **3·2 mJ** ✓
**The check against ½LI².** For this solenoid, L = µ₀n²Al = (4π x 10⁻⁷)(1·6 x 10⁷)
(3·14 x 10⁻⁴)(1) = **6·3 mH** ✓ and ½LI² = **3·2 mJ** ✓ exactly matching - confirming
that ½LI² is just the field energy integrated over the volume.
**The electrical analogue.**
magnetic: u = **B²/2µ₀** ✓
electric: u = **½ε₀E²** ✓
Both quadratic in the field, and in an electromagnetic wave the two are **equal**.
**Reading the distractors.** **32π** ✗ and **6·4π** ✗ are ten times and twice the
answer - errors in the turn density or in the factor of 2. **1·6π** ✗ is half ✓
∴ 3.2 π.

A rotating rod develops **½ωBL²**, and the ten spokes are in **parallel** - so the emf
is the same as for one.
**Step 1 — find the emf of a single spoke.** Each element at radius r moves at v = ωr
and contributes
dε = B(ωr)dr ✓
Integrating from 0 to L:
**ε = ½ωBL²** ✓
**Step 2 — see what the other spokes do.** All ten rotate identically, so each develops
the **same** emf, and all are connected between the **same two points** - the axle and
the rim ✓ They are in **parallel**.
**Step 3 — conclude.** Identical sources in parallel give the emf of **one** of them:
**ε = ½ωBL²** ✓ independent of N.
**Why parallel sources do not add.** Adding emfs requires a **series** connection ✓
Ten identical cells in parallel still give one cell's voltage - though they can supply
ten times the current, since the internal resistance is divided by ten.
**Why the 10 is in the question.** Purely as a distractor ✓ Two of the four options
carry a factor N, and both are wrong for exactly this reason.
**Where the ½ comes from.** The **outer** parts of the spoke move faster than the inner
parts ✓ The average speed over the length is ωL/2, so
ε = B(average speed)(length) = B(ωL/2)(L) = **½ωBL²** ✓
**The flux view, which is quicker.** In one revolution the spoke sweeps the whole disc,
area **πL²** ✓ so
ε = ΔΦ/Δt = BπL²/(2π/ω) = **½ωBL²** ✓ the same answer in one line.
**Which end is positive.** By F̄ = qv̄ x B̄, positive charge is driven **outward** for
the usual field direction ✓ so the **rim** becomes positive and the axle negative -
reversing if either B or ω is reversed.
**A worked instance.** L = 0·5 m, ω = 100 rad s⁻¹, B = 0·1 T:
ε = ½(100)(0·1)(0·25) = **1·25 V** ✓
**Where this appears in practice.** The **homopolar generator** or Faraday disc ✓ a
copper disc spun in an axial field, which produces a large current at a very low
voltage - used for electromagnetic launchers and as a laboratory standard.
**Reading the distractors.** The two options with **N** ✗ treat the spokes as being in
series. **ωBL²** ✗ omits the factor of ½ from the averaging ✓
∴ ½ ωBL².
